prompt:
(a) Let $u$ and $v$ be two nilpotent elements in a commutative ring (with or without unity). Prove that $u+v$ is also nilpotent. (An element $u$ is called nilpotent if there exists a positive integer $n$ for which $u^n=0$.)

(b) Show an example of a (non-commutative) ring $R$ and nilpotent elements $u,v\in R$ such that $u+v$ is not nilpotent.
answer: (a) If $u^n=v^m=0$, every term of the binomial expansion of $(u+v)^{n+m}$ contains $u^i$ with $i\ge n$ or $v^j$ with $j\ge m$. (b) In $2\times2$ matrices, $u=E_{12}$, $v=E_{21}$ have $u^2=v^2=0$ but $(u+v)^2=I$.

solutions.title: Binomial theorem; matrix units
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $u^n=0$ and $v^m=0$; then $u^i=0$ for $i\ge n$ and $v^j=0$ for $j\ge m$. In a commutative ring the binomial theorem holds (with the integer coefficients understood as repeated sums, so no unity is needed):
$$(u+v)^{n+m}=\sum_{i=0}^{n+m}\binom{n+m}{i}u^iv^{n+m-i}\qquad(\text{with }u^0v^{k}:=v^k,\ u^kv^0:=u^k).$$
In each term either $i\ge n$, or $i\le n-1$ and then $n+m-i\ge m+1$. So every term is $0$, and $(u+v)^{n+m}=0$.

**(b)** Let $R$ be the ring of real (or integer) $2\times2$ matrices and
$$u=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad v=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $u^2=v^2=0$, but $u+v=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $(u+v)^2=I$, so $(u+v)^k\in\{I,\,u+v\}$ is never $0$. (Another example from the official solutions: $u=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$, $v=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ with $u^2=v^2=0$ and $(u+v)^2=-4I$.) ∎

prompt: Let $(G,\cdot)$ be a finite group of order $n$. Show that each element of $G$ is a square if and only if $n$ is odd.
answer: If $n$ is odd, every $g$ has odd order $m$ and $g=(g^{(m+1)/2})^2$. If $n$ is even, there is an element $t$ of order $2$ (pair each element with its inverse), so $t^2=1^2$ and the squaring map is not injective, hence (by finiteness) not surjective.

solutions.title: Odd orders; an element of order 2
solutions.body:
**$n$ odd ⇒ every element is a square.** Let $g\in G$ have order $m$. By Lagrange's theorem $m\mid n$, so $m$ is odd and $\frac{m+1}2$ is an integer. Then
$$\big(g^{(m+1)/2}\big)^2=g^{m+1}=g^m\cdot g=g .$$

**$n$ even ⇒ some element is not a square.** First, $G$ has an element of order $2$: the sets $\{g,g^{-1}\}$ partition $G$; each has $2$ elements unless $g=g^{-1}$, i.e. $g^2=1$. The set $\{1\}$ has one element, and $n$ is even, so there must be another one-element set $\{t\}$ with $t\ne1$, $t^2=1$.

Now the squaring map $s\colon G\to G$, $s(x)=x^2$, satisfies $s(t)=1=s(1)$ with $t\ne1$, so it is not injective. A map from a finite set to itself is injective iff it is surjective, so $s$ is not surjective: some element of $G$ is not a square. ∎

solutions.title: Counting with the 2-part of the order (official idea)
solutions.body:
For the direction "$n$ even ⇒ not all squares", here is another argument. Let $2^e$ ($e\ge1$) be the largest power of $2$ dividing the order of some element of $G$ (such elements exist: by the pairing argument there is an element of order $2$). Pick $h$ with $\operatorname{ord}(h)=2^e u$, $u$ odd. Suppose $h=k^2$. Then $\operatorname{ord}(k)$ divides $2\operatorname{ord}(h)=2^{e+1}u$ (since $k^{2^{e+1}u}=h^{2^eu}=1$) but does not divide $2^eu$ (since $k^{2^eu}=h^{2^{e-1}u}\ne1$). Hence $2^{e+1}\mid\operatorname{ord}(k)$, contradicting the maximality of $e$. So $h$ is not a square.

The direction "$n$ odd ⇒ all squares" is as in the first solution: $g=(g^{(m+1)/2})^2$ with $m=\operatorname{ord}(g)$ odd. ∎

prompt:
For a function $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ the secant of $f$ at points $a,b\in[0,1]$, $a<b$, is the line in $\mathbb R^2$ passing through $(a,f(a))$ and $(b,f(b))$. A function is said to intersect its secant at $a,b$ if there exists a point $c\in(a,b)$ such that $(c,f(c))$ lies on the secant of $f$ at $a,b$.

1. Find the set $\mathcal F$ of all continuous functions $f$ such that for any $a,b\in[0,1]$, $a<b$, the function $f$ intersects its secant at $a,b$.
2. Does there exist a continuous function $f\notin\mathcal F$ such that for any rational $a,b\in[0,1]$, $a<b$, the function $f$ intersects its secant at $a,b$?
answer: 1. $\mathcal F$ consists exactly of the affine functions $f(x)=\alpha x+\beta$. 2. Yes: e.g. $f(x)=\sum_k4^{-k}h(x-q_k)$ with $h(t)=\sqrt{|t|}\sin\ln|t|$ and $(q_k)$ an enumeration of $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$; its right difference quotients at every rational point take arbitrarily large values of both signs.

solutions.title: Level sets near a maximum; infinite Dini derivatives at rationals
solutions.body:
*(The official solutions leave this problem blank; this solution is our own.)*

Subtracting an affine function $\ell$ from $f$ does not change the property "intersects its secant at $a,b$": the secant of $f-\ell$ is the secant of $f$ minus $\ell$. So $f$ intersects its secant at $a,b$ iff $g=f-L_{ab}$ has a zero in $(a,b)$, where $L_{ab}$ is the secant.

**Part 1: $\mathcal F$ = affine functions.** Affine functions lie on all their secants, so they belong to $\mathcal F$. Conversely let $f$ be continuous and not affine. Let $L$ be the secant at $0,1$ and $g=f-L$; then $g(0)=g(1)=0$ and $g\not\equiv0$ (otherwise $f=L$ would be affine). Replacing $f$ by $-f$ if necessary, $M=\max g>0$; let $p$ be a point with $g(p)=M$, and fix $t\in(0,M)$. Let
$$a=\max\{x\in[0,p]: g(x)\le t\},\qquad b=\min\{x\in[p,1]: g(x)\le t\}$$
(these sets are closed and contain $0$, resp. $1$). Then $a<p<b$, $g(a)=g(b)=t$ by continuity, and $g>t$ on $(a,b)$. The secant of $g$ at $a,b$ is the horizontal line $y=t$, and $g$ never meets it on $(a,b)$. So $g$, and hence $f=g+L$, does not intersect its secant at $a,b$, and $f\notin\mathcal F$.

**Part 2: yes.** *A sufficient condition.* Suppose $f$ is continuous and for every rational $a\in[0,1)$
$$\limsup_{t\to0^+}\frac{f(a+t)-f(a)}t=+\infty,\qquad\liminf_{t\to0^+}\frac{f(a+t)-f(a)}t=-\infty .\tag{$*$}$$
Take rationals $a<b$, let $s$ be the slope of the secant and $g(x)=f(x)-f(a)-s(x-a)$. Then $g(a)=g(b)=0$ and $\frac{g(a+t)}{t}=\frac{f(a+t)-f(a)}t-s$ takes positive and negative values for arbitrarily small $t>0$. So $g$ has a positive value and a negative value at points of $(a,b)$, and by the intermediate value theorem a zero strictly between them, in $(a,b)$: $f$ intersects its secant at $a,b$. Moreover such an $f$ is not differentiable at rational points, so it is not affine, i.e. $f\notin\mathcal F$.

*Construction.* Let $h(t)=\sqrt{|t|}\,\sin(\ln|t|)$ for $t\ne0$, $h(0)=0$. Then $|h(t)|\le\sqrt{|t|}$, $h$ is $C^1$ on $t\ne0$ with $|h'(t)|=|t|^{-1/2}\big|\tfrac12\sin\ln|t|+\cos\ln|t|\big|\le\tfrac32|t|^{-1/2}$, and
$$|h(u)-h(v)|\le3\sqrt{|u-v|}\qquad\text{for all }u,v.\tag{H}$$
*Proof of (H):* write $d=|u-v|$. If $u,v$ have opposite signs (or one is $0$), $|h(u)-h(v)|\le\sqrt{|u|}+\sqrt{|v|}\le2\sqrt d$. If $0<v<u$ (the negative case is symmetric): when $v\le d$, $|h(u)-h(v)|\le\sqrt{2d}+\sqrt d\le3\sqrt d$; when $v>d$, the mean value theorem gives $|h(u)-h(v)|\le d\cdot\tfrac32v^{-1/2}<\tfrac32\sqrt d$.

Let $q_1,q_2,\dots$ enumerate $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$ and
$$f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty4^{-k}h(x-q_k),\qquad x\in[0,1].$$
Since $|h(x-q_k)|\le1$, the series converges uniformly and $f$ is continuous.

*Verification of $(*)$.* Fix $m$ and $a=q_m<1$. For small $t>0$ split
$$\frac{f(a+t)-f(a)}t=\underbrace{4^{-m}\frac{h(t)}{t}}_{\text{main}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k\le m+1,\,k\ne m}4^{-k}\frac{h(a+t-q_k)-h(a-q_k)}{t}}_{\text{finite part}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k>m+1}4^{-k}\frac{h(a+t-q_k)-h(a-q_k)}{t}}_{\text{tail}} .$$
The finite part converges as $t\to0^+$ (each $h(\cdot-q_k)$ with $q_k\ne a$ is differentiable at $a$), so it is bounded by some $B$ for small $t$. By (H) the tail is at most $3\sqrt t\sum_{k>m+1}4^{-k}/t=\frac{4^{-m}}{4}\,t^{-1/2}$ in absolute value. The main term equals $4^{-m}t^{-1/2}\sin\ln t$. Along $t_j=e^{\pi/2-2\pi j}$ ($\sin\ln t_j=1$) the quotient is at least $\frac34\,4^{-m}t_j^{-1/2}-B\to+\infty$, and along $s_j=e^{-\pi/2-2\pi j}$ ($\sin\ln s_j=-1$) it is at most $-\frac34\,4^{-m}s_j^{-1/2}+B\to-\infty$. So $(*)$ holds at every rational $a\in[0,1)$.

Hence this $f$ is continuous, not in $\mathcal F$, and intersects its secant at every pair of rational points $a<b$.

**Answer:** 1. $\mathcal F=\{x\mapsto\alpha x+\beta\}$ (affine functions). 2. Yes. ∎

prompt:
Let $f\colon[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be a strictly convex continuous function such that
$$\lim_{x\to+\infty}\frac{f(x)}{x}=+\infty .$$
Prove that the improper integral $\int_0^{+\infty}\sin\big(f(x)\big)\,dx$ is convergent but not absolutely convergent.
answer: Eventually $f$ increases to $\infty$ with right derivative $\to\infty$; with $x_k=f^{-1}(k\pi)$ the integral becomes an alternating series $\sum(-1)^kI_k$ where, by concavity of $f^{-1}$, $I_k$ decreases to $0$ (Leibniz) while $I_k\ge\frac13(x_{k+2}-x_{k+1})$ with $x_k\to\infty$, so $\sum I_k=\infty$.

solutions.title: Alternating series via the concave inverse
solutions.body:
*(The official solutions leave this problem blank; this solution is our own.)*

**Step 1: behaviour of $f$.** A convex function has a non-decreasing right derivative $f'_+$ on $(0,\infty)$ and $f(y)-f(x)\ge f'_+(x)(y-x)$ for $y>x>0$. If $f'_+$ were bounded by $M$, then $f(x)\le f(1)+M(x-1)$ for $x\ge1$, contradicting $f(x)/x\to\infty$. Hence $f'_+(x)\to+\infty$. Choose $x_*$ with $f'_+(x_*)>0$; then $f$ is strictly increasing on $[x_*,\infty)$ (as $f(y)-f(x)\ge f'_+(x)(y-x)>0$ for $y>x\ge x_*$) and $f(x)\to\infty$. Let $g=f^{-1}\colon[f(x_*),\infty)\to[x_*,\infty)$, continuous, increasing, $g(y)\to\infty$.

**Step 2: $g$ is concave.** For $u<v<w$ in the domain put $a=g(u)<b=g(v)<c=g(w)$. Convexity of $f$ gives $\frac{v-u}{b-a}\le\frac{w-v}{c-b}$, i.e. $\frac{b-a}{v-u}\ge\frac{c-b}{w-v}$: the slopes of $g$ decrease, so $g$ is concave. Consequently, for fixed $\ell>0$ the function $y\mapsto g(y+\ell)-g(y)$ is non-increasing.

**Step 3: the alternating series.** Let $K$ be an integer with $K\pi\ge f(x_*)$ and $x_k=g(k\pi)$ for $k\ge K$. On $[x_k,x_{k+1}]$, $f$ increases from $k\pi$ to $(k+1)\pi$, so $\sin f$ has the constant sign $(-1)^k$ there. Put
$$I_k=\int_{x_k}^{x_{k+1}}|\sin f(x)|\,dx,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\int_{x_K}^{x_N}\sin f(x)\,dx=\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}(-1)^kI_k .$$

*$I_k\to0$:* $\pi=f(x_{k+1})-f(x_k)\ge f'_+(x_k)(x_{k+1}-x_k)$, so $I_k\le x_{k+1}-x_k\le\pi/f'_+(x_k)\to0$.

*$I_k$ is non-increasing:* by Fubini, $I_k=\int_0^1\lambda_k(s)\,ds$ where $\lambda_k(s)$ is the length of $\{x\in[x_k,x_{k+1}]:|\sin f(x)|>s\}$. With $\alpha=\arcsin s\in[0,\frac\pi2)$, this set is $\{x: k\pi+\alpha<f(x)<(k+1)\pi-\alpha\}$, an interval of length
$$\lambda_k(s)=g\big((k+1)\pi-\alpha\big)-g\big(k\pi+\alpha\big).$$
By Step 2 (with $\ell=\pi-2\alpha$), $\lambda_{k+1}(s)\le\lambda_k(s)$ for every $s$, hence $I_{k+1}\le I_k$.

By the Leibniz criterion, $\sum(-1)^kI_k$ converges. For $X\in[x_k,x_{k+1}]$, $\int_{x_K}^X\sin f$ differs from the partial sum $\sum_{j=K}^{k-1}(-1)^jI_j$ by at most $I_k\to0$; together with the finite integral over $[0,x_K]$, the improper integral $\int_0^\infty\sin f(x)\,dx$ converges.

**Step 4: no absolute convergence.** For $0\le s\le\frac12$ we have $\alpha\le\frac\pi6$, so the interval $[k\pi+\alpha,(k+1)\pi-\alpha]$ has length $\ge\frac{2\pi}3$ and lies to the left of $[(k+1)\pi,(k+2)\pi]$. As the slopes of the concave $g$ decrease, the average slope of $g$ on the first interval is at least that on the second:
$$\lambda_k(s)\ge\frac{2\pi/3}{\pi}\big(g((k+2)\pi)-g((k+1)\pi)\big)=\frac23(x_{k+2}-x_{k+1}).$$
Hence $I_k\ge\int_0^{1/2}\lambda_k(s)\,ds\ge\frac13(x_{k+2}-x_{k+1})$ and
$$\int_{x_K}^{x_N}|\sin f(x)|\,dx=\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}I_k\ge\frac13\big(x_{N+1}-x_{K+1}\big)\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\infty,$$
since $x_N=g(N\pi)\to\infty$. So $\int_0^\infty|\sin f(x)|\,dx=\infty$. ∎

*Remark.* Strict convexity is not needed; convexity and $f(x)/x\to\infty$ suffice. Example: $\int_0^\infty\sin(x^2)\,dx=\sqrt{\pi/8}$ converges but not absolutely.
